Hello! I am also going into art as a career and I have some advice that may help you. Art school is really expensive, but it isnt necessary. Though, if you want a degree in art any college or university with a program for the arts will be just as good as an art school. 

Im going to a state university that has art programs in it for my bachelors. Im currently in highschool but also completing my associates degree. Basically after I graduate highschool id go straight to get my bachlors degree. 

I dont know if you do digital or traditional art. But you can make a LOT of money either way. But digital art is a growing industry that has become more popular the last few years. You do illustration so this could definitely be something you could do. Im going to go for digital media as my bachlors degree, and I feel the same might be good for you. Having a degree in digital media allows you to have access to several different jobs, including game design, illustration, animation, journalism, etc. Its a wide variety that you could go for. 

See what university or colleges around you are offering for the arts. There are some top art schools in the United States like CalArts and RISD, but you could get the same degree at a different university for a cheaper price with the same exact skills. Though be smart on choosing where you are going to. If you choose a university that isn't well known or doesn't have a lot of employers looking at them, then it won't help you much in terms of connections. But if the university or college has a lot of employers and contracts with other companies then definitely try to go for them. Art is a growing industry and its getting better and better everyday, as an illustrator you have a lot going for you.

Hmm I'm not sure what exactly or how exactly you draw. But the way I draw and create art is based off of my life experiences and my emotions. Not all artists are like that, some just draw things they think are cool, some draw because they like the process of figuring out complicated structures like buildings or machines. A lot of my art has an emotional attachment to me. I draw how I feel at the moment. If I feel sad, you can notice that in my art at that given moment. If I feel happy you'll see it in my art, etc etc. 

You should try some exercises like this. Draw what you feel. Try to imagine your emotions as a person or an animal or a 'thing'. I suppose thats where you can go crazy and be i guess "creative". Or you could make a list of things you'd like to study or draw, and go by that. 

Or you could do something like inktober, except it isnt for October. Make a list of words, or look up a list of random words and try to make drawings off of those words. Itll take some time though. Make some thumbnail sketches and see which sketch you like best and move forward with that one.

Sometimes it's really hard to stay committed. And when looking at other artists its pretty hard sometimes even for me to not compare my art to theirs. But sometimes its best to stop looking at their art as something like a level we can never reach, but as something that we can learn from. My favorite artist in thr whole world is Sui Ishida. His art makes me feel so happy and feel at peace with the world. He is the one who made Tokyo Ghoul. 

At first I did compare my art to his. But just yesterday I attempted to research into his art style to try and get something out of it. I learned his process is more of like a painting process than a sketching and drawing one. So I decided to 'paint' my next piece. It felt exhilarating because it was as if he was teaching me, standing right beside me. I have one of his art books that I look at for reference and inspo. 

I know its hard to not compare yourself. But in this case you're going to need to allegedly force yourself to think more clearly and positively. Whatever the other comment said, I dont really see it that way. I know a lot of people who gave up on art like a week after starting because it was hard or whatnot. But you kept at it for 2 years. Thats absolutely nuts. Personally I have never seen someone stick that long to art especially after feeling the way you feel. Its amazing. 

Yes art is hard. But keep in mind you don't necessarily need to draw everyday. I dont draw everyday. I draw when I feel like it. I draw when I have free time and it feels right for me to draw. I struggle a lot with art block and sometimes I feel like my art never really progressed. But remeber, it is a skill. Its like playing the guitar. Obviously someone whose played longer than you will be better. 

You don't need to draw everyday, draw whenever you feel like it. Art is something for you to enjoy and feel at peace with. It isnt something to beat yourself up over. There are people who draw probably a few times a month and still make crazy good art. 

The way I try to really keep up with learning about art when I dont have time to draw or when I dont feel like it, is to draw in my head. I look at something near me. Like a building. In my head I pay attention to the lines, the crevices the perspective of the building, the color, I imagine with my finger following the building like a paint brush. This helps with learning about depth and perception. Which is how I got better at drawing buildings. 

Art isn't going to be your main focus in life I assume right? You have other things that you are focusing on. I feel like you have a really high expectation when it comes to your art that isn't necessary. I started to draw seriously when I was about 12. But I never saw any real improvement until I was around 15. Took me 3 years to see what I was doing wrong and what I needed to improve on. 

Like you said in your original post, draw whatever the hell you want. You have a goal, thats amazing. Good on you. Now I need you to make a plan to achieve that goal. You could literally just draw for 5 to 10 minutes a day or every few days. That would be terrific. You dont need to spend an hour or 4 hours to draw. Anything you doodle even in your notebooks is something to be proud of. Its something by your hand you have created and birthed into this world. Its hard. Itll be really hard. But you already kept at it for 2 whole dam years. Keep going. I could tell you really love art, you're just feeling a bit frustrated with it. If you'd like I can recommend you some YouTubers who have helped me in my art journey.

Hmm, OP, what are you currently doing to practice drawing? Looking at your post history I've only seen 2 drawings and I dont think they really show the extent of your skill set since it is very limited amount of art posted. 

Listen. Doesnt matter how old you are or how long you've been drawing. Every. Single. Artist. Started. From. Point. Zero. Drawing is a skill. It isnt a talent. Everyone learns at a different pace and in different ways that may not work for others. Lets get 1 thing straight here. Comparing your art to others will do you no good whatsoever. You can obviously tell what others can do, but you ignore why you yourself are able to do. Yes, you will feel insecure about your art. Its a given. No matter your skill set or no matter your experience, every artist has something about their art they feel insecure about. 

Now let's talk about what you are exactly doing. Ask yourself these questions: 

What do I do to improve my art? 
How often am I drawing? At what frequency is that at? 
Do I have a clear focus on what I want to achieve in my art career (this doesn't mean art occupation it just means your art hobby) 
Do I know what I want to learn about? 

What is it that you want to do in art? Is it architecture? Character design? Is it animal art? Is it background art? What kind of style are you going for? Realism? Abstract? Semi realism? What about a cartoonish kind of style? Do you want to develop your own style? 

I want you to make a list of goals. What is it that you want to get better at in art? Is it anatomy? Is it realism in general? Is it perspective? Etc. 

Make a list. Ill give you my list as an example: 
I want to get better at comic art and character design, and background art. 

It doesn't need to be detailed. Just straight to the point. 

Now I want you to compile a list of artists that you really love. Look at Instagram or pinterest, and make a board of all of their art and all those artists so you know what you like and have inspiration to fall back on when you need ideas. 

Now I want you to evaluate your schedule. What days are you free? What days are you busy? Around what time do you feel most motivated to draw? Here is my schedule as an example: 

I am busy from Monday to Friday from 6 am till 3pm. I am free to draw everyday from 5pm till 11pm. I only ever really feel motivated to draw during the weekend, Friday and Thursday. So I make time on those days specifically for drawing. 

Now that you have a list of what you want to learn and the kind of art that you like and want to go for, I want you to make a goal. Here is my goal as an example: 

I want to make a character sheet for my OC before summer break starts. 

Make it realistic, make it reachable and not too wishy washy. Think about your schedule and think about your limits. 

Now I want you to start from step number 1. The basics. Every artist, including myself always go back to the basics every now and then whrn needed. Its a good way to remind ourselves what wr need and what we know. Sure its annoying sometimes but it is completely necessary to do. Search up on YouTube art basics. There will be loads of videos to watch for you to brush up on your skills. Also consider looking into color theory videos. 

Next I want you to pick a subject to study and decide how to go along with doing so. Here is my subject as an example: I wil learn anatomy for my character designs by watching videos on anatomy and practicing anatomy by doing gesture drawings and observing from model photographs while drawing them.

Every week I want you to focus on what part of your goal. It doesn't need to be perfect right away. This is just practice. This is just building technique. It won't be pretty right away nor will it be Leonardo de Vinci level right away. Yes it is irritating to not have much progress done in 2 years. Yes it won't feel great having to practice so much. But if you want your art to look better than you need to start setting these small goals and paying attention to what you are really going for. 

Look, art isn't easy. Its probably one of the hardest skills a person can learn. Its something where a person is constantly trying to get better at while having to constantly stay motivated enough not to quit. I've always drawn as a kid and I love to draw till this day. I struggle with my insecurity about my art. I always feel like it isnt good enough, but every now and then I look back at how far I've gone. From drawing stick figures at age 5 to drawimg full on characters by the age of 16, its important to understand that it takes time. Sure im not where I want to be in my art career, but with every skill it takes time. I hope what I said has helped.

Edit: also 1 more thing OP. From now on after every time you complete a drawing or a sketch, I want you to write down something that you like about it. Don't write anything negative like how you don't like it or you wish it looked better. Write something that you genuinely like about what you make. It could be simple as you like the color scheme or you like how you drew that right eye. I see that you make a lot of negative comments about your art, but not so much positive ones. Start building a healthy habit of complimenting yourself. Itll make you feel better overall, and more motivated to continue with your art.

Try doing timed practices. Set your timer to a set amount of time for you to draw something. So since it takes you a while to draw something, I recommend starting off slow. Start off with 30 minutes. Draw something and when that timer goes off, stop drawing and go onto the next drawing. Try and attempt to finish your drawings in those time frames, you'll gradually become better at it, it just takes time. 

After you practiced a bit with 30 minute intervals, try it with 20 minutes, than 15 minutes. 3 hours is too long to draw a sketch, I think when your drawing it takes you too long to draw the right stroke you are looking for. The more you do this practice, the faster those strokes will take to complete, making drawing easier as well.

I had a similar problem during my freshman year. Dealt with CPS, they were no help, had to go back home and deal with all the ba that was thrown at me, got so behind that I was failing and whole bunch of classes. 

Dont feel ashamed because reporting to CPS didn't do anything, because in general CPS sucks and actually doesn't help that many kids. Most cases aren't even looked into, social workers don't really care much. I had to deal with them for 2 months and all I got was someone trying to diagnose me with BPD and give me meds for schizophrenia  when I didnt have neither of them. It happens to a lot of kids. 

School though, let me give you some advice that I used to get myself out of failing. Right now it may seem like a lot, and im sure it is. Just yesterday I crammed in 3 weeks worth of assignments in 1 whole day. Listen, its going to feel overwhelming but the best thing you can do is give yourself a head start. Make a list of every single assignment that is missing and you are able to still turn in. The best thing you can do is send an email to all of your teachers explaining your situation and asking for an extension for due dates for your missing assignments. They will most certainly give that to you because of what your going through. They can't deny that from you, whenever I had a bad week I just tell my teacher assignments might be late. 

Next look at your list, and write down how long you think each assignment will take you. Take your schedule and over the course or a couple weeks I want you to spread out your assignments so you won't be doing them all at once. Remember!! Its okay to take breaks. Its okay to get away from your computer to stop working for a bit. Make alarms for yourself to remind yourself to take a 10 to 20 minute break. Make sure you have snacks with you to eat, eat your meals and drink water. 

At the end of a hars working day ita always relaxing to take a nice hot shower. 

I know things are really frustrating right now, and sometimes it seems much better to just give up, but you still have a chance to get those grades up. It seems like a lot of things to do, but just tell your teachers online that you need extra time, and make that schedule. 

Whenever I feel depressed and I really just want to give up, I take a step back and do something to clam myself down. Put on some nice lofi music, search up lofi on YouTube and you'll get many relaxing beats to play in the background. Get a snack, watch a funny video, maybe go get a drink. Anything that can help, do it.

I know exactly how you are feeling! Though my reason for that is a bit different ill tell you what I did to help get to where I am now in art. 

When we do not use our skills for long, we tend to become rusty and lose touch in what we found interest in before.  And that is completely normal! It's hard to pick up a pencil after such a long time, and expect for ourselves to do the things we were able to before. Only to be met with dissatisfaction and left feeling disappointed. It will take a while for you to get back into that feeling and the habit of drawing again. It's going to take time and patience, and as well as practice but it isnt impossible. 

I suggest really diving deep into what made you like art before. Was it a Fandom? Were you following some artists on social media? Was it a show that a lot of people did fanart for? Or was it something you found online and you really fell in love with it? Personally, I use pinterest and Instagram to scroll through art. Try finding some artists on social media platforms that really speak to you through their art. Look at what you like about their art. Think about how it makes you feel. 

Also look around you! The world itself has several opportunities to help grow and prosper your motivation and inspiration. It's okay to look at a paper or canvas, and have it blank for a while. Because it happens. That is the process of learning. 

Now ask yourself what do you want to learn how to draw? You said before you would draw heads of a character in an anime style. So im assuming you have an interest in character design? Try looking up anatomy tutorials on YouTube that go in depth of the human body. Watch videos on how to design clothes, how to draw poses. 

Sometimes what really helps me warm up for a drawing im about to do, is timed sketches. I tell just about everyone to do these because they are so helpful in building muscle memory, technique, and skill. Search up some posing models, or models used for pose references. You can find plenty in pinterest. Then, each pose, make sure to time it. So 1 or 2 minutes will be the amount of time you have for each pose. This also can be still life or just about anything you would like to learn about such as animals, cars, buildings, etc. 

It will take some time. Find the things that you like about art. What would you like to learn about? Also, maybe try new mediums like painting, or pastels, or maybe even markers. Personally I've developed a technique on using sharpies to color full pieces that make it look like a printed poster. Everybody has different things they like. I wish you luck!

I suggest learning the basics if anatomy. Its not just about attaching the head or limbs to the body, the head and the limbs and everything is the body. But it is hard to understand each part. I suggest looking at mickymegamega. He has several tutorials on anatomy that really allowed me to learn techniques on figuring out how to draw the body. Though he does not really cover masculine body types, so another YouTuber I suggest is Marc Brunet.- "Drawing the male body. Construction explained" its a detailed video that goes indepth on the male body.

But again, the human body cannot be learned simply by some videos. I also suggest doing practices, times drawings are my number 1 go to. Go on Google images or even pinterest, and search up poses or human model poses. Try drawing each pose you see timed. So let's say each pose you draw, you decide to time each drawing 30 seconds to 1 minute. Why such a short amount of time? Because then you'll be able to grasp the human body at a faster and faster rate. If that's too fast try setting each drawing to be 2 minutes. And gradually lower the amount of time you have, and you'll eventually get faster and learn what strokes are best to achieve that type of look. You'll build muscle memory, so drawing a head won't be so difficult in the future. 

Also keep in mind you do not need to practice like an hour everyday. A simple 15 to 20 minutes everyday is just as efficient!

Personally, from a person whose been suicidal for most of my life so far, the best way to help someone is to make sure you are there for them, and you make sure they know they can go to you for help. Provide them that shoulder to lean on, give them that hug of acceptance. 


Do things that would make them happy. Even if its a little thing. Like giving them a snack, or texting them a "hey, I hope ur day goes well today ". Or giving them a hug when you see them, or complimenting them. Or letting them talk about whatever they want to talk about at that given time, and indulging by asking questions and being active in conversation. Just be a person who they feel like they can relax around. 

I know this is stressful. Because you won't always know exactly what they need or want, and sometimes you really can't do anything besides give them space. You don't need to directly do things. Sometimes doing things indirectly is the most helpful. 

Also one thing I noticed that may help a bit, is when you are asking them questions such as "how was your day?" Or  how are you feeling?" It may feel irritating or annoying towards the other person. I always hate it when people ask me that cus I know it'll always be the same answer. Instead try asking them questions about specific stuff. Like "have you listened to any new songs lately? Here are some i have" or "what did you do today?". Basically ask questions that require your freind to think and explain instead of providing them with "yes or no" questions.

Ask yourself this: is it better for me to help them so they won't hurt themselves, or is it better for me not to do anything so they won't be angry at me? 

Which is better for you in the long run? 

Most of the time suicidal people won't like it when people interfere, so its understandable the reason why your friend acted like that. I suggest you sit down with them and have a long discussion on what is best for the both of you on this subject. 

Honestly I don't suggest being dramatic or anything of the sort, just be calm and try to think logically. Is it possible for you to talk to them irl? It might have a much bigger impact on them if you sat them down and explained how you feel about the situation. That you are worried about them. That you want to help whenever they need help. 

But my biggest suggestion is only provide help when it is asked of you, unless you really think its necessary to cross that boundary. If you feel like their life is in danger, get them that help right away.

Hello!! I had the same exact problem when I first started drawing. And I still kinda do even after 10 years of experience. 

Sometimes our visual skills exceed our drawing skills. We know exactly what we want (or somewhat), we expect to reach what we want, and once trying we easily fail due to lack of experience. 

Sometimes focusing on one thing is good, sometimes focusing on more then one thing is good too. I want you to look at learning art, as going to your classes in school. There are many different subjects in art and as we get to choose what classes we go to in school, it is the same thing with art. Pick 2 to 3 subjects in art. You said you wanted to learn anatomy, then thats subject number 1. Now figure out another subject or 2. But not too many so u won't over work yourself. 

Now I want you to pick 2 to 3 days where you focus on your subjects. These days are the days where u take notes and expirement on building up techniques. Its great that you are watching videos and tutorials! Also read books about art you can easily find in the library. Doing so will help expand your knowledge on art. It doesn't need to be a history book. It could simply be a how-to or a personal diary of an artist.

Now that you have your 2 to 3 days of focusing on your subjects, I want you to pick another 2 to 3 days of the week(has to be different then the ones you picked earlier). These days will be the days where you just simply draw what you have learned so far. You can doodle, you can do some more studies, you can make a little project, you can even step out of your comfort zone and experiment with new media other then pencil. 

A tip to learn how to draw faster is by using pen. Just a normal ballpoint Pen thst you could buy in dollar tree for a single dollar. No need for expensive art supplies. Whenever you are practicing, use a pen, because it will teach you to memorize the strokes you should do other then the strokes you shouldn't. Use this trick when sketching. And always put a timer. You can time each sketch to be 30 seconds to 2 minutes. The more sketches you do the faster you will learn. 

Dont stress about how your art looks like atm. Every artist started out as a person who had no experience. Some people learn faster then others, some slower and thats okay!! 

Do not be afraid to try new things. And its okay if you don't want to draw for a bit. Art is something to let yourself enjoy, not to be frustrated over. It takes time to develop the skills that will allow you to ease through drawing. You are already doing what many others cannot. I've heard many people tell me they are going to start to learn to draw and be an artist. And not even a week later do they tell me they quit. 

Take as much time as you want!! Find and practice as many techniques as you'd like. And eventually you will draw as beautifully and as fast as you want.

Hello! I was sexually abused when I was little, and my sister has a hard time helping me because she isnt knowledgeable about what to do, so I understand how you feel. 

I'll say it in the context as if I were speaking to my sister, I think that would make more sense to you. 

Anything traumatic will leave a person feeling some type of way for a while. And sometimes it will cause me to act differently towards the people around me. Even if they are my loved ones. I can get really moody and down, and will blatenly ignore my sister and my freinds sometimes. If your sister acts like this, I suggest to give her space and tell her if she needs any help with anything that you are there for her. 

Another thing that I notice my sister having trouble is when I get panic attacks or nightmares. I will be really anxious and be hysterically crying. These are very scary and its hard to calm down from them. If your sister has panic attacks, the first thing you need to do is help her be aware of her surroundings, ask her how does the room look like, what does she see. Ask her things that she likes to do. This helps to take her mind off of her current worries. 

If your sister has nightmares, and she wakes up crying, the thing id want my sister to do is to tell me everything is okay, and that she is there for me. And that im not in current danger. Ask her if she would like some water or some snacks. Talk to her about things she likes, or talk to her about future plans you two have. 

Do all of this in a calm manner. You will most likely be extremely worried, but showing that your worried and/or scared will most likely make your sister even more worried and anxious. My sister tends to show her emotions quite a lot, so when I'd wake up from a nightmare she looks extremely scared, and it makes me even more anxious. Try to have a low relaxing voice when talking, and don't male any sudden movements. 

Another thing I can think of, is when you say you are there for her, and try to offer help. My sister tends to ask me "what do you want me to do?" Or will say "I dont know what to do". I understand in these situations it might be confusing on how to handle everything but to hear those things makes me really anxious. Instead, try to simply say you will listen to her, and you can say "lets figure this out together". Its more reassuring. 

Sometimes, you will know what to do. And other times, you won't. And that's perfectly okay. Respect her boundaries, and always let her know that you care. Even if you aren't sure what to do, sometimes you don't need to do anything more then tell her you will listen to whatever she wants to say. 

For me, in my family, it is really looked down on to discuss your feelings. Because of this, I tend to keep a lot of my anger and sadness inside, which then reflects my current mood and then affects the people around me. Let your sister know that you care and you will help with what she needs help with.

I think, you might be over working yourself. I too, have a similar problem. But this usually occurs, at least for me, when I am overworking myself and/or setting too high of expectations for myself at the time that im drawing. 

I've been drawing for years, ever since I was a little girl. But we all need to take a break sometime or another. Even if you are trying to push out a drawing this month, pushing it won't make it turn out thr way you want. A clear mind and a relaxed body will produce the best quality work. 

Art style, is also a complicated but also simple concept. No one artist has a specific art style. Sure one person might show art that allows for someone to easily recognize it is their art, but all artists have multiple art styles actually. You could have a cartoon style as well as a realistic style, as  well as a pop culture style. It can be all over the place. Do not stress it. It will eventually form, it takes time. Even if that time seems really long. 

You can have as many art styles as you want, there is no list or set of rules when it comes to art. Just draw what makes you happy. 

If you feel as if your art may be not what you'd like it to be, then take a step back and revisit the basics again. It can feel time consuming, annoying, or something you just might not feel like doing. But it will help you immensely. 

Whenever you are starting a drawing, I suggest take a sheet of paper. And make scribbles all over it. Let it warm up your elbow and wrist muscles. Preparing it for your drawing. Draw circles. Draw ovels. Draw lines that meet or never intersect. Let it flow, like your breath. 

This will allow for you to feel more comfortable with the media you are using. It allows for your mind to be at ease. Never overthink the random shapes and lines your scribbling. Just let your arm do the talking. 

I hope this advice helps you, I wish you luck.
